subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prospect Theory in Investing
description: A fast breakdown of Prospect Theory in Investing for builders.

hook.text: Investors sell winning stocks too early and hold losing stocks too long. Prospect theory predicted this exactly.

buildup.text: Selling winners locks in a gain, which feels good. Holding losers avoids realizing a loss, which feels terrible.

discovery.text: Shefrin and Statman called this the disposition effect. It costs investors about 4% annually in missed returns.

twist.text: Tax laws reward the opposite: sell losers for tax benefits and hold winners for long-term gains. Emotion fights math.

climax.text: Set rules in advance: sell when criteria are met, not when pain or pleasure tells you to. Rules beat feelings.

punchline.text: In investing, your gut is your worst advisor.

quiz.question: What is the disposition effect?
options: Selling winners too early and holding losers too long
Always selling at the right time

details.summary: Prospect theory explains why investors hold losing stocks too long hoping to break even and sell winning stocks too quickly to lock in gains. This disposition effect costs investors billions annually by systematically selling winners and keeping losers.
details.whyItMatters: The disposition effect is one of the most costly behavioral biases in finance. Understanding it helps investors override their instinct to avoid realizing losses and instead make decisions based on future prospects.
takeaways: Investors sell winners prematurely and hold losers too long
Loss aversion makes realizing a loss feel twice as painful as gains feel good
The disposition effect reduces portfolio returns by 3 to 5 percent annually

faq.question: Why do investors hold losing stocks?
faq.answer: Selling at a loss makes the loss feel real and permanent. As long as the stock is held, the loss is only on paper and recovery feels possible. Loss aversion creates a powerful emotional resistance to accepting a realized loss.

faq.question: How can investors overcome the disposition effect?
faq.answer: Set predetermined stop-loss rules before buying. Evaluate each position by asking whether you would buy it today at the current price. Automate rebalancing to remove emotion. Focus on after-tax returns rather than individual gains and losses.
